additions.text: Pablo is new in a parcel warehouse. He writes the labels and the cards: the parcel, the box, the book, the table. Today Elena, the supervisor, finds three mistakes on his cards. By the end of the class you know if a word is masculine (el, un) or feminine (la, una), even when the ending tricks you.
the book · a parcel
the table · a box
The problem is serious; the hand is small.
In Spanish, a table or a book is also masculine or feminine. It is not about meaning: it is grammar. The article (el, la, un, una) tells you the gender.
“La caja” (the box): masculine or feminine?
“Un paquete” (a parcel): masculine or feminine?
“El problema” ends in -a. Is it feminine?
Masculine: el, un
The phone is on the table.
A glass is for Elena.
The colour of the box is blue.
Feminine: la, una
The label is on the box.
The address is correct.
The destination city is Quito.
Do not learn “paquete”: learn “el paquete”. Do not learn “llave”: learn “la llave”. That way you never hesitate.
the television
the engine
the university
the flower
Tricky words: the ending lies
The problem is the address.
The language of the label is Spanish.
The day is long in the warehouse.
The photo of the parcel is on the card.
The delivery rider’s motorbike is in the street.
Look at the sentences: the problem is “serio”, the hand is “pequeña”. The describing word changes with the gender (-o / -a). Today you only notice it; you practise it in class 006.
the problem
a hand
the language
“Crema” (cream) ends in -ma. Is it masculine, like “problema”?
Feminine words that start with a stressed a
The water is cold.
Classroom 12 is new.
The shipping area is closed.
The school classrooms are big.
the water in the bottle
the warehouse alarm
the school classrooms
The map is in the box.
The photo is of Quito.
Area B is closed.
Good morning, Pablo. Are the cards ready for the shipping area?
Yes, here they are. There are three: a parcel for Quito, a box for Lima and another box for a school.
Let’s see. Card one: “la problema de la dirección”. No, Pablo: it’s “el problema”.
“El problema”? But it ends in -a!
Yes, but it’s masculine, like “el tema” or “el día”. Card two: “un mapa de Lima y un mano de madera”.
What’s wrong? “Un mapa” is correct, isn’t it?
Yes, the map is fine. But it’s “una mano”: “la mano” is feminine.
Oh, of course: like “la foto” or “la moto”. They end in -o, but they’re feminine.
Exactly. Card three: “paquete para la aula 12”. It’s “el aula”, Pablo.
“El aula”? So it’s masculine?
No, it’s feminine: “el aula nueva”. It’s like “el agua fría”: “el” only because of the sound.
Got it. I’ll correct the three cards now. Thanks, Elena!
How many cards does Elena check?
What is wrong on card two?
Why is it “el aula”?
Pablo prepares more labels for the warehouse. Which article does each word take?
Contents: an alarm system.
The climate in Lima is humid.
The catalogue photo is on the table.
Which is the customer’s language: Spanish or Portuguese?
Parcel for the University of Cusco.
Contents: a hand cream.
The system is new.
The motorbike is in the street.
Why does Elena call?
Where is the big parcel going?
What is in the parcel?
What is the problem?
Where is the water for the office?
Masculine: -o, -or (almost always)
Feminine: -a, -ción, -dad
Tricky words: learn them by heart
Feminine words with el: still feminine
The ending helps almost always, but the article is the boss. Learn every word with “el” or “la”: el problema, la mano, el agua fría.
Now in a school: a teacher prepares the list for her classroom. Correct her list.
You now know if a word is masculine or feminine. The natural next step: el, la, los, las and un, una, unos, unas, and when to use each one. With gender clear, choosing the article is easy.

Lucía works at a small company with two offices: one in the city centre and one by the harbour. Today she is preparing the supplies order: pencils, notebooks, folders, clocks… For the order she needs the plural: more than one thing.
a red pencil · a blue folder · a clock
two red pencils · two blue folders · two clocks
From “dos” (2) on, the noun is plural. The numbers themselves do not change: dos lápices, dos carpetas.
“Dos carpetas azules”: how many folders?
“A red pencil” → “two…”
To make the plural, look at the last letter of the noun. Is it a vowel (a, e, o)? Add -s. Is it a consonant (l, r, n, d, j…)? Add -es.
Does it end in a vowel? Add -s.
a chair → two chairs
a notebook → three notebooks
a table → four tables
the map → the maps
Does it end in a consonant? Add -es.
a city → two cities
a clock → two clocks
a sheet of paper → lots of papers
a computer → five computers (in Latin America: computadora)
a lamp → two…
a marker → three…
a city → two…
Does it end in z? Change z to c and add -es.
a pencil → two pencils
a light → three lights
once → twice (one time → two times)
a light → two…
the meeting → the…
Monday → Mondays
Is the noun plural? Then the article and the adjective are plural too.
the red pencil → the red pencils
a blue folder → some blue folders
the white lamp → the white lamps
a big clock → some big clocks
the green folders
some big clocks
the new maps
Which one is correct? (four small notebooks)
Which one is correct? (some green lights)
Hi, Diego! Are you at the office? I’m preparing the supplies order for the two offices.
Yes, I’m here. For the harbour office: eight pencils and two clocks for the wall.
Eight pencils? What colour?
Red. And some blue folders for the contracts.
Perfect. And for the meeting room? Some lamps?
Yes, three white lamps. The lamps we have now are broken.
Great. The city-centre office needs markers for the whiteboard and notebooks.
Big notebooks or small ones?
Small notebooks. And two city maps for the entrance.
And the lights in the corridor? Are they OK?
Yes, the lights are fine. The order goes out next Monday.
Great! Thanks, Lucía.
What does the harbour office need for the wall?
Why do they need new lamps?
What do they NOT need in the order?
a printer → two printers
a big box → two big boxes
the city maps
Ten red pencils.
The blue folders are on the table.
Two white clocks for the meeting room.
The corridor lights are fine.
Why is Diego calling?
How many pencils does the harbour office need now?
What are the clocks like?
What does Marta need?
What about the chairs?
after a vowel: add -s
after a consonant: add -es
z changes to c
the whole group agrees
Look at the last letter: vowel → -s; consonant → -es; z → -ces. Then make the whole group plural: article, noun and adjective. Gender does not change: el mapa → los mapas.
For the meeting room: three new lamps.
We need two clocks for the corridor.
Ten green pencils, please.
Some white papers.
Today you made short groups plural: “dos lápices rojos”. In class 006 you look closely at adjectives: how they describe things and how they agree in gender and number, even with two nouns together.

Irene Salas is an estate agent. Today she and her colleague Pablo are rewriting the listings for two apartments: one on calle Olivo and one on calle Río. To describe a home well, you need to know where the adjective goes.
It is a big apartment, with a white kitchen.
It is a great apartment in a good neighbourhood.
In “una cocina blanca”, the adjective goes…
“Un gran apartamento” mainly gives…
Noun + adjective: the neutral order
It is a small bedroom.
The listing has a nice photo.
It is a quiet street.
The owner is a Colombian man.
They are two big windows.
A listing for the website: “Living room with a green rug”.
Irene talks about the owner: “She is a Peruvian lady”.
“A round table” in Spanish is…
Adjective + noun: an opinion, a highlight
It is a good price.
It is a great terrace.
Today is a bad day to visit homes: it is raining.
It is a good area to live in.
It is a good apartment for a family.
It is a great kitchen!
It is a bad time to sell: the building is under renovation.
With a few adjectives, the position changes the meaning. After the noun, the basic meaning. Before the noun, another meaning. Today you learn four very frequent pairs.
Don Ramón is 85: he is an elderly friend.
Ana is 32, but she is an old friend of Irene: friends from school.
To talk about a person’s age, “viejo” can sound harsh. “Mayor” is kinder: “un señor mayor”. “Un viejo amigo”, on the other hand, is always something nice.
“Es el único apartamento con terraza” means…
“Un apartamento nuevo” is…
Irene and Carlos have been friends for twenty years. Carlos is…
Which sentence is right?
Pablo, look at the photos of calle Olivo. It is a great apartment.
Yes, and it is a big apartment: ninety square metres.
Exactly. With a bright living room and a white kitchen.
And the building? Is it new?
No, it is an old building, from 1950. But the kitchen is new.
And the owner? Is he a client of the agency?
It is don Ramón, an old friend of my family.
And the apartment on calle Río?
It is a brand-new apartment, small, but it is the only apartment in the building with a terrace.
So it is a unique apartment. And it is in a good neighbourhood!
Perfect. Now, the two listings: the normal adjective, after the noun.
How many square metres is the calle Olivo apartment?
Who is don Ramón?
Why is the calle Río apartment special?
Living room with a blue sofa.
It is a great offer!
It is a good price for the neighbourhood.
The owner is a Mexican lady.
It is the only apartment with a garage.
It is a bright living room.
It is the only apartment with a balcony.
Why is Irene calling?
What is the living room on calle Olivo like?
What does Irene say about the price?
What is special about the calle Río apartment?
After the noun: the neutral order to describe.
Before the noun: your opinion, with a short form.
Same adjective, another meaning before the noun.
After “es”: always the basic meaning.
If you describe, the adjective goes after: una cocina blanca. Before the noun only to give an opinion (gran, buen) or with a special meaning: un viejo amigo, el único apartamento.
The agency is also selling a small hotel on the beach. Write three pieces of its listing.

You can now describe and rate an apartment. Next you need to point: this apartment, that balcony, that building over there. In class 008 you learn to say which thing you mean, near or far from you, with the same agreement as today.

Marta Ríos hosts “Gente nueva”, a cultural centre’s podcast. Today she interviews three new members of the conversation group: Elena, Pablo and Ana. The game: each person introduces someone else. For that you need the verb ser.
She is Elena. She is a doctor.
She is from Chile. She is Chilean.
She is very calm.
“Es médica” tells you…
“Es de Chile” tells you…
For “she is calm” (her personality), you say…
to be: who, what, where from, what like
I am Marta Ríos and I am a journalist.
My sister is a doctor and she is from Chile.
Pablo and I are Colombian.
Ana and Elena are very nice.
Are you from Medellín?
As you know, the verb shows who: “Somos amigos” = “Nosotros somos amigos”. Use the pronoun to clarify or contrast: “She is Chilean and he is Colombian”.
We are from Valparaíso.
Are you Mr Herrera?
My parents are teachers.
Pablo and his brother are from Medellín.
jobs: no “a / an” in Spanish
Pablo is a teacher.
Pablo is a very patient teacher.
Ana is an engineer. Her brother is a lawyer.
I am a student. Leo is a journalist.
“Elena es de Chile” = “Elena es chilena”. With de you use the country or the city; without de, the nationality adjective, which agrees with the person.
Ana is an engineer.
Pablo is a very fun teacher.
Elena is Chilean.
Ana and her sister are Brazilian.
You know estoy from the first class. Today, just one contrast: ser says who a person is; estar says how they are today.
Elena is a doctor. She is calm.
Today Elena is tired.
After twelve hours at the hospital: “I am tired”.
Elena presents her job: “I am a doctor”.
Pablo talks about Ana: “She is very nice”.
Which sentence is correct?
Good afternoon and welcome to Gente nueva. Today there are four of us in the studio.
The introductions are crossed. Pablo, who is she?
She is Elena Rojas. She is from Valparaíso: she is Chilean. And she is a doctor.
How interesting! Elena, your turn: what is Pablo like?
Pablo is a music teacher and he is Colombian, from Medellín. He is an excellent teacher and he is very funny.
Thanks, Elena! And now Ana. Ana, you are from Brazil, right?
Yes, I am Brazilian, from Recife. I am an engineer. And today I am a bit nervous: it is my first interview in Spanish.
Relax, Ana! We are friends here. What are Elena and Pablo like?
They are very nice. Elena is calm and Pablo is very chatty.
Perfect! Three people, three countries and one group.
Where is Elena from?
What is Ana’s job?
Why does Ana say “estoy nerviosa” and not “soy nerviosa”?
My sister and I are doctors.
Pablo, are you from Medellín or Bogotá?
You are the host, right?
Ana and Pablo are very nice.
I am a journalist and I am Mexican.
She is an engineer.
Ana is Brazilian.
Elena is an excellent doctor.
We are from Colombia.
What is this audio?
What is Elena’s job?
Where is Pablo from?
How is Ana feeling today?
Who introduces Ana?
who someone is and their job
with an adjective, add un / una
where someone is from
what someone is like
how someone feels today
Name, job, origin, nationality and personality: ser. A bare job takes no “a”. Nationality agrees and is lowercase. How you feel today: estar.
A health conference in Lima. A participant’s name badge says: Dr Carmen Soto · paediatrician · Quito (Ecuador). You introduce her.
Carmen and her colleague Dr Ruiz, also from Quito: “They are Ecuadorian”.
You can now say who someone is with ser. Today you saw just one contrast: “Estoy cansada”. In class 012 you study estar in depth: how you feel and where you are. That completes the ser / estar pair.

Lucía is an engineer. This week she is in Monterrey for work. Her brother Daniel is in Mexico City, at home with their mum. On the call, the two key questions are “Where are you?” and “How are you?”. Both use the verb estar.
I am in Monterrey, at the hotel.
I am tired, but happy.
I am an engineer.
“Estoy en Monterrey” tells you…
“Estoy cansada” tells you…
“Soy ingeniera” uses…
Estar is irregular but easy: “estoy” is special, and the other forms carry an accent on the a (except estamos).
“Está” with an accent is the verb: Mum is at home. “Esta” without an accent means “this” (class 008): this house. You can hear it too: es-TÁ / ES-ta.
Daniel and Mum are at home.
I am in Monterrey.
Mum is in the kitchen.
how you are: feelings, physical state
Mum is nervous today.
Are you busy, Daniel?
My colleague Ana is sick.
Mum and I are calm.
Lucía: “Today I am very tired”.
Daniel and Mum are happy.
How are you? — I am fine, thanks.
where someone or something is
I am at the hotel.
Daniel is at home, with Mum.
The keys are here.
The hotel is near the station.
Monterrey is far from Mexico City.
Lucía, at the hotel: “I am here”.
Lucía asks about the keys, which are at Daniel’s place: “Are they there?”
In class 011 you learnt ser: who you are, your job, where you are from. With ser you also say what someone is like in general. With estar you say how they are today and where they are.
Mum is a calm person.
Mum is calm today.
Daniel is usually a very calm person.
Today Mum is not calm.
Lucía is from Mexico City, but now she is in Monterrey.
Which sentence is correct?
Hello? Hi, Lucía! Where are you?
Hi, Daniel. I am in Monterrey, at the hotel. It is a quiet hotel.
And how are you?
I am tired, but happy. And you? Are you at home?
Yes, I am here, at home, with Mum. Mum is a bit nervous today.
Nervous? But Mum is a very calm person.
Yes, but today she is not calm. Her keys are not on the table.
Relax. The keys are in the kitchen, near the window. Are they there?
Yes, they are here! Now Mum and I are calm.
Great! Monterrey is far away, but on Sunday I am home. A kiss for Mum.
Where is Lucía?
How is Mum today, and why?
Where are the keys?
Mum and I are at home.
Are you busy now?
Today I am sick.
My suitcases are at the hotel.
Are you all OK?
The hotel is not far.
Daniel and I are tired.
What is this audio?
What is the hotel like?
How is Lucía?
Who is sick today?
Where is Lucía’s passport?
how you are now
who someone is and what they are like
“Es tranquilo”: that is how he always is. “Está tranquilo hoy”: that is how he is right now. And a location always takes estar: “estoy en Monterrey”, never “soy en”.
Where are you now?
My parents are in Monterrey.
Daniel is a very calm person, but today he is nervous.
Lucía and Ana are tired.
You can now say where a person or a thing is: “The keys are in the kitchen”. In class 013 you learn “hay” (there is / there are) to say what exists in a place, and when to use hay or estar.
Paula Medina is at the San Rafael Clinic in Bogotá with her son Leo. At reception there is a form: name, age and symptoms. For almost the whole form, Paula uses one verb: tener (to have).
I am thirty (years old).
I am cold and I am sleepy.
I have an appointment at ten.
For age and for cold, heat, hunger, thirst and sleepiness, English uses “to be”: I am 30, I am cold. Spanish uses tener: literally “I have 30 years”, “I have cold”.
“Tengo treinta años” tells you…
“Tengo frío” tells you…
In “Tengo una cita”, Paula has…
Tener is irregular. “Tengo” has a g. “Tienes, tiene, tienen” change e to ie. “Tenemos” and “tenéis” are regular.
In Argentina and Uruguay, with “vos”, the form is “tenés”: “¿Vos tenés frío?”. It means the same as “¿Tú tienes frío?”. In this class you use “tú tienes”; “tenés” is just for recognising it.
Leo is six.
Paula and Leo have an appointment.
Madam, do you have your ID?
“¿Vos tenés frío?” means…
How old are you?
I am thirty.
The doctor is forty-five.
My mother is sixty-eight.
How old are you? — I am twenty-two.
Paula is thirty.
Paula is from Argentina.
You ask a friend his age:
My grandma is seventy.
What do you feel?
I am very thirsty. Is there any water?
Leo is hot.
We are very sleepy.
I am hungry: the cafeteria is on the first floor.
I am sleepy.
I am tired.
There is no food at home: Leo is hungry.
It’s a hard week: Paula is tired.
I am very thirsty.
Leo is very cold.
Which one is correct?
Good morning. Your name, please?
Paula Medina. I have an appointment at ten with Dr Ruiz.
Very good. Here is the form. How old are you?
I am thirty. I am from Argentina, but I live here, in Bogotá.
And the boy? Is he your son?
Yes, this is Leo. He is six.
Now, the symptoms. How are you today?
I am cold and I am sleepy. And I am tired.
And Leo? Is he cold too?
No, he is hot. And he is very thirsty.
There is water near the window. Do you have your ID, please?
Yes, here it is. And I have a question: where is the bathroom?
How old is Paula?
What symptoms does Leo have?
At the end, what does Paula have?
Good morning, Paula. What’s wrong today?
I have a headache and I am very cold.
And you are tired, right?
Yes, very tired. It’s a hard week.
Hi, Leo. And you, are you hungry?
Yes! I am very hungry. And I have a dinosaur.
How nice! Paula, it’s nothing serious: lots of water and early to bed.
Dr Ruiz is forty-five.
Paula and Leo are hungry.
Paula is very tired.
Are you thirsty? There is water here.
I am thirty-two.
Leo is very thirsty.
I am tired and I am cold.
What is this audio?
Who has priority?
Where do children under twelve wait?
What is there for people who are cold?
Where is the cafeteria?
Who has all the answers?
age: I am thirty. How old are you?
how your body feels: I am very thirsty. Leo is hot.
to have something: I have an appointment at ten.
origin and state: I am from Argentina. I am tired.

If in English you say “I am 30” or “I am cold / hungry / thirsty / sleepy”, in Spanish you say “tengo”. If it is an adjective ending in -o / -a (tired, nervous), use estar. And for “very” with a noun: mucho / mucha, not “muy”.
My son is eight.
I am from Colombia, but I live in Madrid.
Open the window, please: I am very hot.
The children are very hungry.
Today my father is very tired.
Now you are not at the clinic: you are at a new gym, filling in your registration form. The rule is the same.

Today you used “mucha hambre” and “mucho frío”: the word changes with the noun. In class 015 you see this rule across the whole noun phrase: article, noun and adjective together, in gender and number (“las manos frías”, “un niño cansado”).

Paula, Hugo and Rosa work in a small design studio in Guadalajara, Mexico. On Monday mornings they look at the week’s agenda together: who is who, where everyone is, where they are going and what meetings they have. For that they use four verbs: ser, estar, ir and tener.
Paula is the coordinator.
Hugo is in the office.
Rosa is going to the bank.
I have two meetings.
“I go to work and I have two meetings.” With these two forms you can already tell your Monday: where you go and what you have.
“Rosa va al banco” tells you…
“Hugo está en la oficina” tells you…
“Tengo dos reuniones” uses…

Ser, estar, ir and tener are irregular: they don’t follow the pattern of hablar, comer and vivir. But they are the most frequent verbs in Spanish, and you will use them every day. You already know ser, estar and tener; ir is new.
With “yo”, three verbs end in -oy: soy, estoy, voy. Tener is different: tengo. And watch the vowel: tienes, tiene, tienen, but tenemos.
In Argentina and Uruguay many people say “vos” instead of “tú”: vos sos, vos estás, vos vas, vos tenés. Today you only need to recognise it; you use tú: eres, estás, vas, tienes.
I am a designer.
We have a meeting at ten.
Paula and Hugo are in the office.
You are going to the bank today.
to go (where to?)
I go to the office at nine.
Are you going to the bank today?
On Tuesday Paula is going to Puebla.
We are going to the meeting room.
Hugo and Rosa go downtown by metro.
With ir, the question is “¿adónde vas?” (where are you going?). With estar, the question is “¿dónde estás?” (where are you?).
On Thursday we are going to the design fair.
Hugo goes to work by bike.
—Where are you going? —To the office.
I’m going to work. (on my way)
I’m at work. (already there)
It’s ten o’clock. Paula is already in the room.
At ten to nine, Hugo leaves home: he is going to the office.
Rosa isn’t answering the phone: she is in a meeting.
Look at the agenda: on Friday I have a meeting with a client.
Which sentence is correct?
Good morning, Hugo. Where is Rosa?
She’s at the bank, with the invoices. Today is Monday: bank day.
Oh, of course. Do you have the agenda for the week?
Yes, here it is. I have two meetings: on Tuesday and on Thursday.
On Tuesday I’m not here: I’m going to Puebla with a client.
And on Wednesday? Are the three of us going downtown?
Yes, to the design fair. Rosa has the tickets.
Hi! Sorry, I’m a bit tired. The bank is chaos on Mondays.
Don’t worry. Look: on Wednesday we’re going to the fair.
Perfect. And on Friday I’m not going to the office: I have the day off.
Great, team. There are three of us and we have a very full week.
Where is Rosa at the beginning?
Where is Paula going on Tuesday?
Who has the tickets for the fair?
I go to the office by bus.
Hugo and Rosa are in the meeting room.
Paula, do you have time today at five?
We are a small team.
Rosa is thirty-two.
Are you two going downtown on Thursday?
I go to work by metro.
We are in the meeting room.
Rosa has three meetings today.
Where are you going on Thursday?
Why is Paula speaking?
Where is Paula on Thursday morning?
When does Hugo have the meeting with the bank?
Where are Paula and Rosa going on Monday?
Where are the new keys?
to be (who / what)
to be (where / how)
to go (where to)
to have
With “yo”: soy, estoy, voy, tengo. And today’s pair: voy al trabajo (I’m moving) / estoy en el trabajo (I’m already there).
Now you use the four verbs outside work: your weekend with your family.

You can now use the four most frequent irregular verbs: soy, estoy, voy, tengo. In class 019 four more verbs arrive with a special “yo” form: hago, pongo, salgo, vengo. With them you can tell your full routine: what time you leave, what you do and where you come from.

Carla, Diego, Paula and Marcos are friends. On Saturday there is a dinner at Carla’s place and everyone has a task. To share out the tasks you need four very common verbs: hacer, poner, salir and venir.
Who does what?
I make the food.
Diego puts the music on.
Marcos leaves work at seven.
Paula comes at seven.
Today I go shopping and leave early.
“Pongo la mesa” means…
“Marcos sale del trabajo” means…
How does the “yo” form of these verbs end?
In class 017 you learned the regular present. Hacer, poner and salir are regular in every person except “yo”. With “yo” they end in -go.
Learn hago, pongo, salgo. For the other persons, use the regular endings.
Traer works the same way: yo traigo, tú traes. Today you only need to recognise it.
I make the dessert for the dinner.
You put the plates on the table.
Diego and Paula leave home at six.
Venir has two changes, just like tener (class 018): -go with “yo”, and -ie- with tú, él and ellos. With nosotros and vosotros it is regular.
In Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America people say “vos”: hacés, ponés, salís, venís. In Spain, for several people, “vosotros”. You use tú and ustedes: everyone understands you.
Carla, are you coming to the dinner on Saturday?
We are coming at seven.
I am coming by bus.
I’m coming from the market. I have the bread.
I’m going to the market. Do you need anything?
When someone calls you and you go towards them, Spanish says “¡Voy!” (I’m coming!).
Carla gets home with the bags: “I’m coming from the market”.
Diego leaves home: “Now I’m going to the market”.
“Marcos is coming from work.”
Which sentence is correct?
Hi, guys! Saturday is the dinner at my place. I’m making the food.
Great! I’ll put the music on.
And I’m making the dessert. Marcos is setting the table, right?
Yes, sure. But on Saturday I leave work at seven.
No problem. What time are you coming?
I’m coming straight from work. I’ll arrive at half past seven.
Perfect. Diego and Paula, you’re coming at seven, right?
Yes. Diego and I leave home at half past six.
Carla, are you doing the shopping?
Yes, on Saturday morning I’m going to the market.
(Saturday, 12:00) I’m coming back from the market with two big bags. I have everything!
Who is making the dessert?
Why does Marcos arrive at half past seven?
In the last message, where is Carla coming from?
I’m making an omelette for the dinner.
What time do you leave work?
Paula and Marcos are coming at seven.
I put the glasses on the table.
I’m coming from the market. I have everything!
I set the table at seven.
I’m coming from the market.
Today I leave home early.
Paula and Diego are coming at seven.
What is the voice message for?
Why is there a change?
Who is setting the table now?
What is Carla making to eat?
What does Carla do in the morning?
What time are Diego and Paula coming?
only the “yo” form ends in -go
the other persons are regular
venir changes like tener
from / to
With “yo”, think -go. With the other persons, regular endings; venir adds -ie- except with nosotros.

You already know the change in vienes, viene, vienen. In class 020 you see that many verbs change their vowel like this: quiero, puedo, pido. With them you can say what you want, what you can do and what you order at dinner.

Clara and Diego are travelling together along the coast of Ecuador. They are in Puerto López, a fishing town. Every morning they decide three things: what to eat, what to do and how much money to spend. They have 100 dollars for two days.
Clara: “I want a coffee and some fruit.”
Clara: “I can’t pay much.”
Diego orders eggs with bread.
“Quiero un café” tells you…
“No puedo pagar mucho” is about…
In a restaurant, “pido una sopa” means…

Querer, poder and pedir have the regular endings from class 017. The special part is the stem: when the stress falls on the stem, its vowel changes. QUIE-ro, PUE-do, PI-do. In nosotros and vosotros the stress moves to the ending (que-RE-mos), so the stem does not change.

In Spain, vosotros does not change: queréis, podéis, pedís. In Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America people use vos, and with vos the stem does not change either: querés, podés, pedís. Today you only recognise it; class 021 covers tú, vos, usted, ustedes and vosotros.
I want to see the sea.
We can pay 100 dollars.
They order fish soup.
Why does “queremos” not change?
to want
I want a white coffee.
Diego wants to see the whales.
Do you want to eat at the market?
can / to be able to
I can pay 40 dollars.
I want a coffee, but I can’t stay long: the tour leaves at nine.
Can you book the hotel?
to order / to ask for
I’ll have a mango juice, please.
Clara always orders the local food.
At the end, we ask for the bill.
I want to eat at the market.
Can you book the tour?
Diego asks for the bill.
I want to order ceviche.
We want to order ceviche.
Clara and I want to see the whales.
Diego can pay for the tour.
Rosa and her boyfriend order rice with fish.
You can pay by card.
Which one is correct?
Good morning. I’m hungry. What do you want for breakfast?
I want a coffee and some fruit. And you, what are you ordering?
I’m having eggs with bread. Hey, there is a whale-watching tour today. Do you want to go?
Yes! We both want to see whales. But how much is it?
Forty dollars each. We have 100 dollars for today and tomorrow.
Phew. Then I can’t pay for the tour and an expensive restaurant.
Don’t worry. After the tour, we can eat at the market. It’s cheap.
Good idea. At the market people order ceviche, right?
Yes, and tourists order encocado: fish in coconut sauce. Can you book the tour?
Yes, I can book now. My friend Rosa and her boyfriend want to come too.
Perfect. Then we’ll ask for the tour for four people.
How much is the tour?
Where do they want to eat after the tour?
How many people is the tour for?
Clara and I want to go to the beach tomorrow.
Can I pay by card here?
Rosa always orders mango juice.
My friends can’t come today.
Diego, what do you want to do this afternoon?
We always ask for the bill at the end.
We want to see the whales.
I can’t pay much.
Clara always orders a coffee.
What is Diego talking about?
What do people order on the island’s beach?
What time does Diego want to meet Clara at the port?
Who else wants to come?
what you want
what you can do
what you order or ask for
outside the boot: no change

First look at who. Yo, tú, él, ella, usted, ellos and ustedes: the stem changes (quiero, puedes, piden). Nosotros and vosotros: no change (queremos, podemos, pedimos). And after querer or poder, the infinitive: quiero pedir.
Rosa and I want to go to the island.
Sorry, I can’t go out today: I’m tired.
In the café, Diego always orders eggs.
Can you (all) pay in cash?
We’d like the bill, please.

You can now say what you want, what you can do and what you order, and you saw that vosotros and vos keep the stem. In class 021 you see when to use tú, vos, usted, ustedes or vosotros, and how the verb changes with each one.

Sofía is organising a visit to the Museo de los Colores in Puebla with twelve colleagues from her office. She goes to the information desk with lots of questions: opening hours, price, address, people. Each question needs a special word, always with a written accent.
When does the museum open?
How much is the ticket?
What is the address?
How many people can go in?
The question word goes first, right after “¿”, and then the verb: “¿Cuándo abre el museo?”. You already know the ¿ ? signs from class 022.
“¿Cuánto cuesta la entrada?” asks about…
Sofía wants to know the time. Which word does she use?
What do all these words have in a question?
Each question word asks for one type of information: a thing, a person, a place, a time, a way or an amount. Choose the word for the answer you expect.

In a question these words are stressed, and the accent shows it. Without the accent, “que”, “cuando”, “donde” or “como” are different words that do not ask anything. The accent is not decoration: it changes the word.
—It is on Reforma Street. What is the question?
—Raúl, the guide. What is the question?
At what time does the shop open?
How much? How many?
How long does the tour last?
How many people are there today?
How many days does the museum open?
How many people are coming?
How many rooms does the museum have?
How many students are coming?
How much is the catalogue?
Which room is the nicest? · Which days does it open?
What is the price? · Which are the new rooms?
There are two tours. Which one do you prefer?

This is the general rule and the most useful one to start with. In some parts of Latin America you also hear “¿cuál sala?” in conversation. And careful: “¿Qué es…?” asks for a definition: “What is a museum?”.
What is the museum’s phone number?
Which days are there guided tours?
There is a big map and a small map. Which one do you want?
“¿Qué es una audioguía?” asks for…
Many question words have a “twin” without an accent that does not ask anything: it joins two ideas in a sentence. Today you only need to recognise them.
Some questions sit inside another sentence: “No sé qué sala es”, “¿Sabe dónde está la tienda?”. Exclamations too: “¡Qué bonito!” (How beautiful!). Today you only need to recognise them.
The sign says that the museum closes at six.
What is there in room three?
“No sé dónde está la tienda.” Why does “dónde” have an accent?
Which one is correct?
Good morning! What do you need?
Good morning. We are a group from my office and we want to visit the museum. When does it open?
Tuesday to Sunday, from ten in the morning to six in the evening.
And how much is the ticket?
Eighty pesos per person. How many people are you?
There are twelve of us. Which days are there guided tours?
On Saturdays and Sundays. There is a short tour and a full tour. Which one do you prefer?
The full one. Who is the guide?
Raúl. He is very nice. What is your name, for the booking?
Sofía Herrera. And where is the entrance for groups?
Here, on the right. The tour starts at eleven. See you on Saturday!
Great! Thank you very much.
How many people are in Sofía’s group?
Which tour does Sofía prefer?
How much is the audio guide?
What are the café’s opening hours?
Which room has the old photos?
Who are Saturday’s guides?
When does the guided tour start? —At eleven.
How many rooms are there in the museum?
Who gives the guided tour?
What time does the café close?
Which is the entrance for groups?
What is the audio?
Which day is the museum closed?
How much is a student ticket?
When are there guided tours?
How many people can go in a group?
Who gives the guided tours?
what / which
who
where / when / how
how much / how many
If it asks, it has an accent. “Cuánto” agrees with the noun (cuántas personas). And as a general tendency: “qué” + noun, “cuál” + es or to choose.
On Saturday, after the museum, Sofía and her group go to the Puebla tourist office. Ask their questions.

You can now ask about opening hours, prices, places and people. But sometimes the answer is “no”: “No, it does not open on Mondays”. In class 024 you learn to make negative sentences and where “no” goes in the sentence.
